المأساة؛ فحين تمتد نيرانها إلى الأسواق المكتظة بالمتبضعين، ومواقع تجمع العابرين، ومصادر المياه التي تقوم عليها حياة الناس، فإنها تتجاوز حدود المواجهة العسكرية لتضع المدنيين في قلب محنة لا ذنب له وحين تتحول طائرة مسيّرة إلى أداة قادرة على تحويل سوق يعجّ بالحركة إلى مشهد من الأشلاء والأنقاض، يغدو السؤال الملحّ: أيُّ غاية عسكرية يمكن أن تبرر تعريض حياة الأبرياء لهذا القدر من الفتك؟ إن السودان لا يحتاج إلى مزيد من الأسلحة التي توسّع رقعة الموت، ولا إلى خطابات تبرر كل خسارة مدنية باسم الضرورات العسكرية؛ بل يحتاج إلى إرادة سياسية تكبح آلة الحرب، وإلى مؤسسات وطنية تستعيد استقلالها عن الاستقطاب، وإلى مسار للعدالة لا يساوم على حقوق الضحايا ولا يستثني أصحاب النفوذ. إن الهجمات المتعاقبة التي شهدتها مناطق سودانية خلال الأيام الأخيرة، وما أُعلن عن سقوط أعداد كبيرة من القتلى والجرحى، تضع قوات الجيش السوداني، بقيادة عبدالفتاح البرهان، أمام مساءلة سياسية وأخلاقية وقانونية لا يجوز الالتفاف عليها بالشعارات العسكرية أو البيانات المقتضبة. فالمعيار الحقيقي لأي عملية عسكرية ليس ما تعلنه القيادة عن أهدافها، بل طبيعة الهدف الذي ضُرب، ومدى التحقق من وجود هدف عسكري، والاحتياطات المتخذة لحماية المدنيين. وتشير التقارير إلى ضربات جوية وهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة طالت مناطق مدنية في غرب السودان، من سوق المواشي بمدينة نيالا إلى منطقة الدبيبات بولاية غرب كردفان، وسط اتهامات للجيش السوداني بالمسؤولية عن هجمات أوقعت أعداداً كبيرة من الضحايا. كما ترد أسماء أسواق ومناطق أخرى، من بينها المجلد والضعين وسوق النعام، في سياق التحذيرات من اتساع نطاق الخطر الذي يتهدد المدنيين. وفي 16 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول 2026، تعرّض سوق المواشي بمدينة نيالا لضربة جوية أوردت تقارير صحفية أنها أسفرت، وفق مصدر طبي نقلت عنه وكالة الصحافة الفرنسية، عن مقتل أكثر من 38 شخصاً وإصابة 47 آخرين، وقد نفّذت مسيّرات الجيش هذا الهجوم، وفق الاتهام الذي يتبناه المقال. لقد تحوّل سوقٌ يقصده الناس طلباً للرزق وقضاء الحاجات اليومية إلى مسرح للفاجعة، حيث تُختزل حياة الأبرياء في لحظات دامية، وتُترك الأسر لمواجهة فقدٍ لا تجبره التعويضات ولا تمحو آثاره بيانات التبرير. وفي منطقة الدبيبات بغرب كردفان، أفادت تقارير صحفية نُشرت في 19 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول بأن ضربة بطائرة مسيّرة قرب سوق ومركز لتجمع المسافرين أودت بحياة عشرات الأشخاص؛ وقد تحدثت تلك التقارير عن مقتل 80 شخصاً في الموقع، إضافة إلى وفاة مصابين نُقلوا إلى المجلد متأثرين بجراحهم. ويتهم المقال الجيش السوداني بتنفيذ الهجوم بدم بارد، في واقعة تستوجب كشف ملابساتها وتحديد المسؤولين عنها، وعدم السماح بأن تُطوى أسماء الضحايا في سجلّ النسيان. إن أخطر ما في استهداف المواقع المدنية أنه لا يكتفي بإزهاق الأرواح، بل يضرب البنية الاجتماعية والاقتصادية التي يتكئ عليها السكان في صراعهم اليومي من أجل البقاء. فالسوق ليس مجرد مساحة للبيع والشراء؛ إنه مورد رزق لعشرات الأسر، وشريان لتدفق الغذاء، ومكان تتقاطع فيه حاجات المزارعين والرعاة والتجار والعمال والنازحين. وحين تتساقط القذائف أو تنقضّ المسيّرات على هذه المساحات، لا تُزهق أرواح الموجودين فيها فحسب، بل تتداعى وراء الضحايا حياة كاملة: أسرة تفقد معيلها، وأطفال يُحرمون من موردهم، وتاجر يخسر رأس ماله، وامرأة تعود إلى بيتها بلا ما اشترته لقوت أبنائها، ومجتمع يزداد هشاشة أمام الجوع والنزوح والخوف. أما مصادر المياه، فإن استهدافها أو تعطيلها يفتح باباً آخر من أبواب المعاناة؛ إذ يحوّل الحصول على الماء إلى رحلة محفوفة بالمخاطر، ويضاعف الأعباء الصحية والإنسانية على الأطفال والنساء وكبار السن. ومن المؤسف أن تتعرض الأسواق، التي يفترض أن تكون فضاءات للرزق والتواصل الاجتماعي، لهجمات يُتهم الجيش السوداني بالوقوف وراءها، في ظل اتهامات بأن تلك الضربات وقعت مع سبق الإصرار والترصد، وباستخفاف بالغ بالأضرار المتوقعة على السكان. وهذه الوقائع تثير شبهة ارتكاب جرائم جسيمة بموجب القانون الدولي الإنساني، وتستدعي التحقيق في مدى انطباق توصيف الإبادة الجماعية، ومحاسبة كل من تثبت مسؤوليته. فالقانون الدولي الإنساني يُلزم أطراف النزاع بالتمييز بين المدنيين والمقاتلين، وبين الأعيان المدنية والأهداف العسكرية، كما يفرض اتخاذ الاحتياطات الممكنة لتقليل الأضرار المدنية، ويحظر الهجمات العشوائية والهجمات التي يُتوقع أن تُحدث خسائر مدنية مفرطة قياساً بالميزة العسكرية المباشرة والملموسة المنتظرة. ولا يجوز أن تصبح الضرورات العسكرية ذريعة مفتوحة لاستباحة الأسواق أو تعريض حياة المدنيين للخطر، كما لا يمكن أن تُعفي الرتب العسكرية أصحاب القرار من المساءلة عن أفعالهم متى ثبتت مسؤوليتهم عنها. ولا يمكن فصل الأزمة السودانية عن تاريخ طويل من تسييس مؤسسات الدولة، وتغليب الولاء التنظيمي على مقتضيات الحكم الرشيد، وإخضاع المجال العام لمنطق الاستقطاب والإقصاء. ومن هنا تبرز مشروعية مساءلة التيارات الإسلامية، بما فيها جماعة الإخوان المسلمين في السودان، عن إرثها السياسي ومواقفها من الحرب والسلام، وعن أي دور تثبته الأدلة في تأجيج الصراع أو عرقلة التسوية. ويرى كاتب المقال أن استهداف المدنيين والمرافق الحيوية يرتبط بنهج متجذر في أدبيات الحركة الإسلامية، وأن تكرار التقارير عن سقوط المدنيين في الأسواق والمناطق المأهولة يضاعف ضرورة مساءلة جيش الإخوان المسلمين التابع لحكومة البرهان. وتضع هذه الوقائع جيش الإخوان بقيادة البرهان أمام مسؤوليات متعددة؛ فالمسؤولية السياسية تقتضي الشفافية، والمسؤولية العسكرية تقتضي تفسير القرارات العملياتية التي أفضت إلى خسائر مدنية جسيمة، أما المسؤولية القانونية فتقتضي إتاحة التحقيق المستقل وعدم عرقلة الوصول إلى الأدلة والشهود. ولا ينبغي أن تتوقف المساءلة عند منفذي الضربات في الميدان، بل يجب أن تمتد إلى كل من يثبت التحقيق صلته بإصدار الأوامر أو التخطيط أو التنفيذ أو التستر على الانتهاكات. وتكتسب الهجمات التي تطال الأسواق ومراكز النقل والمرافق الحيوية خطورة إضافية حين تقع في مناطق متاخمة لحدود دولية أو في مناطق ذات وضع سياسي وأمني خاص، مثل أبيي، التي يرتبط وضعها باتفاقات وترتيبات بين السودان وجنوب السودان. ففي 20 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول 2026، أفادت تقارير لوكالتي أسوشيتد برس ورويترز بمقتل ما لا يقل عن 153 شخصاً في ضربة بطائرة مسيّرة استهدفت سوق أُمِّيت في منطقة أبيي المتنازع عليها، وأشعلت حريقاً في مستودع للوقود. واتهم مسؤولون في أبيي الجيش السوداني بتنفيذ الضربة. وتبرز هذه الواقعة، بما تحمله من حصيلة بشرية أولية جسيمة، خطورة استهداف التجمعات المدنية واتساع دائرة التهديد. إن خطورة هذه التطورات لا تنحصر في عدد الضحايا، مهما بلغ، بل تمتد إلى تهديد الروابط الاقتصادية والاجتماعية بين المجتمعات الحدودية، وتعميق الاحتقان بين السودان وجنوب السودان، وفتح المجال أمام مزيد من التوتر الإقليمي. وكلما اتسعت دائرة الهجمات غير المنضبطة، ازدادت احتمالات انتقال آثار الحرب من داخل السودان إلى محيطه، في منطقة تعاني أصلاً من هشاشة أمنية وتحديات إنسانية متشابكة. وحين يدفع المدنيون ثمن الصراع من أرواحهم وأرزاقهم وأمنهم، فإن المسألة لا تعود شأناً عسكرياً داخلياً فحسب، بل تصبح امتحاناً لفاعلية المنظومة الدولية في حماية الإنسان وصون الحد الأدنى من قواعد الحرب. لقد آن للأمم المتحدة ومجلس الأمن الدولي والاتحاد الأفريقي والاتحاد الأوروبي والهيئة الحكومية الدولية المعنية بالتنمية (إيغاد) أن تتعامل مع حماية المدنيين في السودان باعتبارها التزاماً عاجلاً، لا بنداً مؤجلاً في بيانات القلق الدبلوماسي. فالإدانة اللفظية، مهما بلغت فصاحتها، لا تعيد إلى الحياة من سقطوا تحت الأنقاض، ولا توفر الماء لمن فقدوا مصادره، ولا ترد إلى النازحين بيوتهم وأسباب استقرارهم. وتقتضي الاستجابة الجادة دعم آليات مستقلة لتقصي الحقائق بشأن الهجمات التي طالت الأسواق والمرافق المدنية، وحفظ الأدلة والشهادات والصور والبيانات المتعلقة بمسارات الطائرات المسيّرة والأهداف التي ضُربت، وتحديد المسؤوليات وفق معايير التحقيق المعترف بها. كما ينبغي الضغط على جميع أطراف النزاع للامتثال للقانون الدولي الإنساني، وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية، وحماية المنشآت الطبية ومصادر المياه والأسواق ومراكز تجمع المدنيين. ويتحمل مجلس الأمن مسؤولية النظر في التدابير التي تتيحها ولايته لوقف الانتهاكات وحماية السكان، بما في ذلك التدابير الموجّهة ضد الأشخاص والجهات التي تثبت مسؤوليتها عن الهجمات غير المشروعة. كما أن للاتحاد الأفريقي وإيغاد دوراً مهماً في دعم مسار سياسي يوقف الحرب، ويحد من التدخلات الخارجية، ويهيئ الأرضية لتسوية مستدامة لا تقوم على فرض الأمر الواقع بقوة السلاح. وينبغي أن تنصبّ المساءلة، في الوقائع التي يتناولها هذا المقال، على جيش الإخوان المسلمين بقيادة البرهان متى كشفت الأدلة عن انتهاكات ارتكبها؛ فحياة المدنيين ليست باتخاذ إجراءات تحول دون تكرارها، وتمنع الإفلات من العقاب، وتدفع الأطراف نحو وقف شامل للأعمال العدائية وتسوية سياسية تحفظ وحدة السودان وكرامة شعبه. إن السوق الذي يُقصف اليوم ليس مجرد مكان سقط فيه ضحايا؛ إنه امتحان لضمير الحرب، واختبار لجدية العالم في حماية الإنسان. ومصادر المياه التي تُهدَّد ليست منشآت هامشية، بل شرايين حياة لا يجوز تحويلها إلى أدوات ضغط أو ساحات استهداف. وبين واجب وقف الحرب وواجب محاسبة المسؤولين عن انتهاكاتها، يبقى المدني السوداني صاحب الحق الأول في الحياة والأمن والكرامة. فلا سلام مع استباحة أرواح الأبرياء، ولا استقرار مع تحويل أرزاق الناس إلى أهداف عسكرية، ولا عدالة ميليشيات ارتكبت جرائم بحق الشعب السوداني، مُجدِّدة الرفض للكيانات الموازية والإجراءات غير المشروعة خارج المؤسسات الرسمية التي تمس وحدة السودان ولا تُعبِّر عن إرادة شعبه. جاء ذلك في كلمة ألقاها المهندس وليد الخريجي نائب وزير الخارجية السعودي، خلال الاجتماع التشاوري السادس بشأن تعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام في السودان، حيث شدَّد على جهود المملكة لوقف إطلاق النار وصون الوحدة والحفاظ على مؤسسات الدولة السودانية وحمايتها من الانهيار. وأوضح الخريجي أن هذه الجهود تستند إلى إعلان جدة للالتزام بحماية المدنيين الموقّع 11 مايو (أيار) 2023، واتفاقية وقف إطلاق النار قصير الأمد، مبيناً أن السعودية تدعم مبادرة المجموعة الخماسية وغيرها من الجهود الإقليمية والدولية للوصول لحل سياسي يحفظ سيادة السودان ووحدته وسلامته أراضيه. وأكد نائب وزير الخارجية أهمية مساندة الحكومة السودانية في جهودها لتهيئة حوار سوداني - سوداني داخل البلاد، مُشدِّداً على مواصلة المملكة العمل من أجل إنهاء الحرب واستعادة الاستقرار في السودان. جانب من الاجتماع التشاوري بشأن تعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام في السودان (الخارجية السعودية) وبيَّن الخريجي أن السعودية أعلنت تقديم 100 مليون دولار لتخفيف معاناة الشعب السوداني، وأطلقت حملة شعبية عبر منصة «ساهم»، حيث تجاوز إجمالي المساعدات السعودية للسودان 3.2 مليار دولار، فضلاً عن دعم إضافي بقيمة 145 مليون دولار. وأضاف أن هذه المساعدات تأتي في إطار خطة الاستجابة الإنسانية في السودان لعام 2026 خلال مشاركتها اجتماع تنسيق العمل الإنساني بشأن أزمة السودان، في برلين بتاريخ 15 أبريل (نيسان) 2026. من جانب آخر، التقى المهندس الخريجي، على هامش الاجتماع، وزيري الخارجية السويسري ألكسندر فازل، والنرويجي أندريس كرافيك، والشيخ شخبوط بن نهيان وزير الدولة بالخارجية الإماراتية، لتعزيز الأمن والسلام في السودان والجهود المبذولة بشأنها، فضلاً عن المستجدات الإقليمية والدولية. مواضيع أخبار السعودية أخبار السودان السعودية الخليج العربي السودان العالم العربي العالم الأكثر قراءة خطاب رسمي وجهه الشيخ محمد بن زايد آل نهيان، رئيس دولة الإمارات، إلى رئاسة الجمعية العامة ومجلس الأمن، وفق الإجراءات المعتمدة لاختيار الأمين العام الجديد للأمم المتحدة. وأكد الشيخ محمد بن زايد، في خطاب الترشيح، ما تتمتع به نسيبة من خبرة واسعة في العمل داخل المنظمة الدولية، وحكمة في التعامل مع التحديات العالمية الراهنة، إلى جانب سجلها الدبلوماسي الحافل بالجهود البنّاءة في مختلف الملفات الدولية. وتملك نسيبة خبرة دبلوماسية تمتد لأكثر من عقد في الأمم المتحدة؛ إذ شغلت منصب المندوبة الدائمة للإمارات لدى المنظمة الدولية بين عامي 2013 و2024، وهي فترة شهدت مشاركتها في عدد من الملفات السياسية والأمنية والإنسانية. وتولت خلال مسيرتها منصب نائبة رئيس الجمعية العامة للأمم المتحدة، ورئاسة المجلس التنفيذي لهيئة الأمم المتحدة للمرأة، كما شاركت في قيادة جهود تعزيز عمل الجمعية العامة وإصلاح مجلس الأمن. وخلال عضوية الإمارات غير الدائمة في مجلس الأمن لعامي 2022 و2023، ترأست نسيبة المجلس مرتين، وأسهمت في مناقشات تناولت قضايا السلم والأمن الدوليين، والعمل الإنساني، والتنمية المستدامة، والمخاطر الأمنية المرتبطة بالتغير المناخي، إلى جانب تمكين المرأة وإصلاح منظومة العمل متعدد الأطراف، بحسب المعلومات الصادرة اليوم. ويأتي الترشيح الإماراتي في مرحلة تشهد فيها الأمم المتحدة نقاشات بشأن مستقبل النظام الدولي متعدد الأطراف، وقدرة المنظمة على التعامل مع الأزمات الجيوسياسية والتحديات الاقتصادية والإنسانية المتزايدة. وفي موازاة ذلك، يواصل مجلس الأمن تقييم المرشَّحين للمنصب عبر جولات من التصويت غير الرسمي، عُقدت أحدثها في 16 أكتوبر (تشرين الأول) الحالي، تمهيداً للتوصل إلى توصية بشأن المرشح الذي سيخلف غوتيريش. وبموجب ميثاق الأمم المتحدة، تتولى الجمعية العامة تعيين الأمين العام بناءً على توصية من مجلس الأمن، على أن تستمر عملية الاختيار خلال الأسابيع المقبلة، قبل بدء ولاية الأمين العام الجديد في الأول من يناير (كانون الثاني) 2027. منافسة دولية على قيادة الأمم المتحدة وتدخل نسيبة سباقاً يضم ستة كارولين رودريغيز بيركيت، وزيرة الخارجية السابقة في غويانا. وتشمل قائمة المرشحين أيضاً ماريا فرناندا إسبينوسا وإيفون آباكي من الإكوادور، وأولارا أوتونو من أوغندا. وكانت غرينسبان قد تصدرت الجولة الأخيرة Speaking at the celebrations on October 20, Abiy praised the courage of Kenyans who fought for independence and those who sacrificed their lives to defend their country. The Ethiopian leader drew parallels between Kenya's struggle for freedom and Ethiopia's historic Battle of Adwa, when Ethiopian forces defeated an invading Italian army in 1896. "Kenya's history of courage and sacrifice resonates deeply with Ethiopia's own story of Adwa, where Ethiopians from every corner of the country united to defend their homeland," Abiy said in a statement posted on X. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "These shared histories remind us that freedom was never given; it was won through courage, unity, and sacrifice." Abiy also called for stronger economic cooperation between Ethiopia and Kenya, identifying clean energy, regional connectivity, telecommunications and trade as key areas for expanding bilateral relations. "As our histories are intertwined, so too must our futures be," he said. "Through the spirit of Medemer, Ethiopia and Kenya must continue building on our existing cooperation in clean energy, connectivity, telecommunications, and trade to create greater opportunities and shared prosperity for our people." Medemer, a concept promoted by Abiy, emphasises unity, cooperation and collective efforts towards national development. Ethiopia and Kenya maintain close diplomatic and economic relations, with cooperation covering infrastructure development, electricity trade, regional security and cross-border connectivity. The two East African neighbours have also worked to strengthen regional economic integration through transport and energy infrastructure projects aimed at improving trade and investment opportunities. Mashujaa Day, celebrated annually on October 20, honours Kenyans who contributed to the country's independence and national development. Abiy concluded his remarks by saluting those recognised during the celebrations. "To all those honoured today, I salute you. Happy Mashujaa Day!" he said. Read the original article on Horn Diplomat . Inside the Growing Danger for Ethiopia's Humanitarian Workers 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — When humanitarian workers travel to the field, they carry more than food, medicine, or information. They carry the hopes of people facing hunger, displacement, illness, and conflict. Yet, the danger increasingly exposes those delivering this assistance. In Ethiopia, humanitarian workers have been killed, kidnapped, threatened, robbed, and caught in crossfire. Some have been abducted for ransom. Others have lost their lives while carrying out routine duties. These are not simply workplace accidents or unfortunate incidents. They raise serious questions about the protection of people who help others survive crises. The question is simple: Who protects the people who protect others? Ethiopia needs to move beyond telling aid workers to be careful. It needs a system that prevents avoidable harm, supports those affected, investigates serious incidents, and ensures that national and local responders are not left to carry the risks alone. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines From kidnappings to drone strikes Consider the death of Mahelet Sitotaw Abera, a staff member of ORDA Ethiopia. On 20 June 2025, she was collecting humanitarian data in Angot District, North Wollo, when she was critically wounded during crossfire between government forces and non-state armed groups. She died later that day. The United Nations condemned her death and called for the protection of humanitarian personnel. In 2024, Ethiopian NGO worker Yared Melese was abducted in North Wollo. His kidnappers demanded a ransom. His death was confirmed in August, according to The New Humanitarian's investigation . The danger is not limited to national organizations. On 24 June 2021, three Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) staff members --María Hernández Matas, Tedros Gebremariam Gebremichael, and Yohannes Halefom Reda--were killed in Tigray. In June 2026, MSF said the families had still not received the findings of a credible and impartial investigation. MSF's internal review had concluded that the clearly identified humanitarian workers were deliberately targeted. These incidents are different. Mahelet died during crossfire, Yared was abducted, and MSF maintains that its colleagues were deliberately targeted. They should not be treated as legally identical. But each raises urgent questions about prevention, protection, and accountability. No one should have to risk their life simply to help others survive." The wider situation remains concerning. On 30 September 2026, the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Ethiopia reported that at least ten humanitarian vehicles had been seized by armed groups between 2025 and 2026, with only two recovered at the time of the statement. The UN also expressed concern about incidents affecting aid personnel, humanitarian assets, and premises. The global picture is equally troubling. According to the Aid Worker Security Database , 713 major incidents affecting aid workers were recorded in 2025, compared with 637 in 2024. A Reuters report published in August 2026 said that 907 aid workers were killed, injured, or kidnapped in 2025. These figures measure different aspects of violence and should not be confused: one counts recorded incidents, while the other counts people affected. On World Humanitarian Day, 19 August 2026 , the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that armed drones were changing the risks faced by humanitarian workers. OCHA reported that 350 aid workers were killed, 322 injured, and 235 kidnapped worldwide in 2025. It also reported that, during the first part of 2026, a further 82 aid workers had been killed, 97 injured, and 39 kidnapped. The message was clear: public condemnation alone is not enough. States and parties to armed conflict must respect international humanitarian law and ensure accountability for violations. This threat has also become a direct concern in Ethiopia. On 20 September 2026, a humanitarian truck carrying approximately 41 tonnes of food assistance for internally displaced people in Sheraro, northwestern Tigray, was reportedly hit during drone strikes while travelling along a road in the region. Addis Standard reported the incident. The truck was transporting food intended for displaced families who depend on humanitarian assistance. Reports differed on the driver's injuries and how much of the cargo was lost, so those details should be treated cautiously. The attack drew international concern. Human Rights Watch reported that the United States condemned the strike on the humanitarian convoy. The incident is a serious warning: when humanitarian transport is hit, the danger extends beyond the driver and the vehicle. Food supplies may be lost, deliveries delayed, and already vulnerable families left waiting for assistance. The available reports establish that the convoy was struck, but responsibility for the attack should not be asserted without reliable evidence. The use of armed drones raises difficult questions for humanitarian protection. A vehicle carrying relief supplies may be exposed to attack even when it is travelling to support civilians. Humanitarian organizations must continually reassess security risks, protect staff and drivers, review routes and movement procedures, and ensure that personnel can stop a journey when conditions become unacceptable. But these measures cannot replace the responsibility of parties to a conflict to respect humanitarian personnel and relief operations under applicable international law. Behind every statistic is a person, a family, and a community that may lose access to essential assistance. Ethiopia needs credible investigations into serious incidents, public accountability where appropriate, and practical measures to prevent attacks from happening again. My Own Experience: Danger does not end when an incident is over My concern about aid-worker safety comes not only from reports and statistics but also from what I personally experienced while travelling through a conflict-affected area. On one occasion, armed men wearing military-style uniforms stopped several vehicles along the road. At first, we assumed they were government security personnel conducting a routine checkpoint inspection. We soon realized they were members of a non-state armed group impersonating security personnel. They ordered all passengers to get off the vehicles and lie face-down in muddy water beside the road. We were forced to remain there, unable to raise our heads, fearing for our lives. When a woman and two male passengers objected to the order, one of the armed men shot them. All three died in front of us. The armed men then took passengers' mobile phones, money, jewelry, watches, and other valuables. Several vehicles, including other buses, were looted. When we were finally released, I discovered that I had lost my laptop, camera, tablet, clothing, and other belongings. More painfully, I lost months of humanitarian assessment data, photographs, field documentation, and research materials. Their loss disrupted my work and meant that valuable information gathered in the field could no longer be used without significant effort to recover or reconstruct it. The effects went beyond material loss. I had witnessed three people being killed and feared for my own life. The experience reminded me that surviving a security incident does not mean its consequences end when the immediate danger passes. I share this experience because incident reports cannot fully capture the human cost of insecurity. Behind the statistics are people whose lives, families, work, and sense of safety are changed forever. When aid workers are attacked or robbed, humanitarian operations and the communities depending on them can also suffer. This must lead to action. Governments and parties to armed conflict must respect humanitarian personnel and their work. Humanitarian organizations and donors must provide realistic resources for staff protection, emergency support, and care for survivors and families. Serious incidents must be investigated, and those responsible must be held accountable where the evidence supports it. Protecting aid workers is not simply about protecting organizations or projects. It is about preserving the lifeline between people in crisis and the assistance they need. No one should have to risk their life simply to help others survive. Why do aid workers remain at risk? There is no single explanation. In conflict areas, humanitarian workers may be caught in fighting, deliberately attacked, kidnapped for ransom, or threatened because their work is misunderstood or politicized. Vehicles, supplies, and equipment may also be seized. Elsewhere, risks may arise from crime, extortion, administrative restrictions, community disputes, misinformation, or pressure from powerful local actors. The danger is not only about the threats workers face. It is also about how organizations prepare for them. Three factors help explain why the same environment can be more dangerous for some workers than for others. First, "threat" refers to the possibility of harm, such as armed violence, kidnapping, or detention. Second, exposure concerns how often and in what circumstances workers encounter that threat. Third, vulnerability describes the factors that make harm more likely or make it harder to prevent and respond to an incident. These are common elements of humanitarian security risk management. The Global Interagency Security Forum's Security to Go toolkit explains how aid organizations can assess risks and strengthen their security arrangements. For example, two organizations may operate in the same district, but one may have reliable communications, updated security information, and emergency medical arrangements, while the other lacks these resources. Their workers may face similar threats but have very different levels of protection. Research and humanitarian security guidance also point to an important responsibility: organizations must consider the risks faced by different groups of workers, including national staff. The Global Interagency Security Forum's guidance on managing the security of aid workers with diverse profiles highlights the relationship between a worker's circumstances, their role, and their organization's responsibility to take reasonable steps to protect them. A staff member may understand the risks and still feel unable to refuse a journey because a deadline is approaching, funding is limited, or a manager expects the activity to proceed. This is why security cannot depend only on an individual worker's judgment or courage. A credible protection system must allow workers to raise concerns, delay travel, and stop an activity when the risks become unacceptable. Managers must take these concerns seriously, and workers must not be unfairly penalized for refusing an unsafe assignment. This responsibility is also reflected in United Nations Security Council Resolution 2730 (2024) , which calls on states and parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and comply with applicable international humanitarian law. Protecting aid workers requires both respect for these legal obligations and practical action by humanitarian organizations to reduce foreseeable risks. Localization Without Resources: Shifting risk, not power National and local organizations are often close to the communities they serve. Their staff speak local languages, understand social relationships, and can reach people whom others may struggle to reach. Their knowledge is an important humanitarian asset. But local knowledge does not make local responders invulnerable. Localization must not mean that local people carry the risk alone." National staffs continue living in conflict-affected areas when international colleagues relocate. Local NGOs are expected to maintain assistance in dangerous locations while decisions about budgets, program deadlines and security arrangements are made elsewhere. Community volunteers, local health workers and informal responders face even greater challenges. They can be the first to respond to an emergency, yet have limited security training, insurance, emergency assistance or formal recognition. This does not mean that all international organizations provide adequate protection or that every national NGO lacks it. The issue is whether protection reflects the risks people actually face, rather than their job title, nationality or employer. Global funding evidence makes this concern difficult to ignore. A May 2026 study by ODI found that just below 10% of international humanitarian funding reached local and national actors directly and indirectly in 2024. Only 3.8% reached them directly. The report also found that local actors often receive shorter, smaller, and more restricted grants than international counterparts. These are global figures, not Ethiopia-specific estimates, but they illustrate the wider financing problem. When local organizations have limited funding for insurance, security management, emergency medical care and staff support, they struggle to protect the people expected to deliver assistance. This is the localization paradox: local actors are encouraged to lead, but the money, authority and protection needed to lead safely may remain elsewhere. As I argued in my earlier Addis Standard article , transferring responsibility to local organizations is not enough if resources and decision-making power do not follow. Localization must not mean transferring risk to local organizations while keeping control and protection resources elsewhere. Public Trust, Community Acceptance: Important, but insufficient substitutes for protection Humanitarian security often relies on three approaches: acceptance, protection, and deterrence. The Global Interagency Security Forum (GISF) identifies these as complementary elements of humanitarian security risk management. Acceptance means building trust with communities and relevant local actors. Organizations explain who they are, why they are present, how assistance is selected, and how people can raise complaints. They listen to concerns and correct mistakes. Protection involves practical measures such as risk assessments, safe travel arrangements, reliable communications, staff training, and emergency plans. Deterrence aims to discourage attacks through appropriate engagement, legal consequences, and action by responsible authorities. These approaches must work together. Community trust cannot replace practical safety measures, and neither can replace accountability. As GISF's guidance on community acceptance explains, acceptance requires sustained relationship-building and cannot be taken for granted. In Ethiopia, elders, religious leaders, women's groups, youth representatives, customary institutions, and local volunteers may help identify tensions, correct misinformation, and resolve disputes before they escalate. When people believe assistance is being distributed unfairly, for example, clear eligibility criteria and accessible complaints processes can help address concerns before they threaten staff safety. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) highlights the value of listening to communities, sharing information, and creating opportunities for feedback. Customary institutions, including the Gadaa system among Oromo communities , also offer lessons in mediation and collective responsibility. Their role must be understood in its specific context. Such institutions can contribute to trust, but they cannot guarantee safety or replace formal legal protection. Acceptance is not equal for everyone. Shared language, religion, ethnicity, or local identity may help some workers build relationships, while others may face suspicion or discrimination. Women may also experience gender-based harassment and other risks linked to how they are perceived. Two workers performing the same task may therefore experience different levels of safety. Organizations must recognize these differences without stereotyping communities or expecting local leaders to put themselves at risk to protect aid workers. Public perceptions also matter. People may question why some households receive assistance while others do not. Rumors, political accusations, and online misinformation can deepen suspicion and, in some circumstances, contribute to threats against humanitarian personnel. Humanitarian Outcomes' Aid Worker Security Report 2025 examines the changing security environment for aid workers, including concerns about declining acceptance and hostile narratives. The ICRC's guidance on harmful information explains how false or misleading information can undermine trust and put humanitarian workers and affected communities at risk. Humanitarian organizations must respond through transparency, accountability, and effective communication. They should explain assistance criteria, listen to complaints, and address legitimate criticism rather than dismiss it. Community radio, local-language discussions, schools, religious leaders, and trusted digital communicators can help explain humanitarian principles and why attacks on aid workers disrupt essential services. Trusted local content producers could help deliver accurate, accessible messages to wider audiences. However, campaigns must avoid political propaganda, protect sensitive information, and ensure that sharing stories or images does not expose staff or communities to further danger. The aim is to encourage informed public discussion, not to silence criticism or portray every critical voice as hostile. Awareness must also reach relevant government institutions, military personnel, and armed actors. Under applicable international humanitarian law, humanitarian relief personnel are entitled to protection in the circumstances set out in the relevant rules. Article 71 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions addresses personnel participating in relief actions, while Rule 31 of the ICRC's Customary IHL Study sets out the customary rule on the protection of humanitarian relief personnel. Public awareness alone is not enough. Training, engagement with authorities and military command structures, credible investigations, and accountability for violations must reinforce these legal obligations. Ultimately, communities can help create a safer environment, and responsible communication can strengthen trust. But humanitarian workers must not be left to depend on goodwill alone. Community acceptance is one part of protection; the responsibility to respect applicable law, protect humanitarian personnel, and hold perpetrators accountable remains essential. From legal promise to practical reality International humanitarian law provides important protection for humanitarian relief personnel during armed conflict, subject to the applicable legal rules. The International Committee of the Red Cross identifies the protection of humanitarian relief personnel in customary international humanitarian law. In May 2024, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2730, calling on states and parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and to address impunity for violations. These protections are not favors. They reflect legal obligations. However, having laws is not the same as enforcing them. Serious incidents must be documented and investigated through appropriate channels. ethiopia.summary: In Ethiopia, humanitarian workers face escalating dangers, including killings, kidnappings, and threats, as they strive to assist those affected by hunger, displacement, and conflict. Recent incidents highlight the urgent need for better protection systems for these workers. For instance, Mahelet Sitotaw Abera was fatally injured in crossfire while collecting humanitarian data, and Yared Melese was abducted for ransom, later confirmed dead. The UN has condemned these attacks, emphasizing the necessity for accountability and protection under international humanitarian law. The situation is exacerbated by armed groups seizing humanitarian vehicles and the use of drones, which pose new risks to aid operations. Reports indicate a significant increase in violence against aid workers globally, with hundreds affected in 2025 alone. The article stresses that protecting humanitarian personnel is crucial not only for their safety but also for the communities relying on their assistance. Effective measures must be implemented to ensure their safety and uphold their vital role in crisis response.

ethiopia.title: Obituary - Prominent Kenyan Oromo Scholar, Anthropologist Professor Abdullahi Shongolo Passes Away

Born in 1958 in Moyale, Kenya, Professor Shongolo completed his education in Kenya. He worked in various parts of the country and served in Kenya's Ministry of Education, rising to the position of Assistant Director of Education. Jaatani Diidaa, a cultural and historical researcher, told Addis Standard that Professor Shongolo devoted much of his life to in-depth research, making significant personal sacrifices to bring the educational and cultural heritage of the Oromo of Kenya and Ethiopia to international attention. Professor Shongolo made substantial contributions to anthropological research, serving as a senior researcher at Germany's renowned Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology for more than two decades, from 1999 to 2019, according to Jaatani. During the 2000s, he also served as an Associate Research Fellow in the Department of Social Anthropology at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden, where he pursued research and academic work. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Among his major scholarly contributions were books co-authored with prominent German scholar Professor Günther Schlee, including Pastoralism and Politics in Northern Kenya and Southern Ethiopia and Islam and Ethnicity in Northern Kenya and Southern Ethiopia . He also documented traditional Borana oral literature and proverbs in Boran Proverbs in Their Cultural Context . These works helped bring greater international recognition to Oromo history, pastoral life, religious traditions, and customary systems of governance, particularly the Oromo customary governance, Gumii Gaayo Assembly. Professor Shongolo's passing "has brought profound grief and shock to the Borana Oromo community, the wider Oromo community across the world, and people in Kenya and Ethiopia, as well as to scholars in the international academic community, Jaatani said. ethiopia.title: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia's rule of law performance has deteriorated further, with the country ranking 133rd out of 143 countries and jurisdictions in the 2026 World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index, according to the ranking provided for this report. The latest assessment extends a multi-year decline that has seen the country remain near the bottom of global and sub-Saharan African comparisons. The 2026 index, released on 21 October, comes as the WJP warns that authoritarian practices are becoming entrenched worldwide, with weakened checks on executive power, declining judicial independence and restrictions on fundamental freedoms contributing to a prolonged global deterioration in the rule of law. The WJP said the global rule-of-law recession had continued for a ninth consecutive year, with 62% of the countries and jurisdictions assessed recording declines, compared with 38% that improved. Although the share of countries experiencing deterioration fell from 68% in 2025, the overall direction remained negative. The latest findings reinforce concerns about institutional accountability and civic freedoms in Ethiopia, where successive editions of the index have documented persistent weaknesses in constraints on government authority, fundamental rights, open government and the enforcement of regulations. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines A sustained decline across successive editions Ethiopia's latest ranking follows a pattern documented by Addis Standard in previous years. In the 2025 edition, the country ranked 132nd out of 143 countries, with its overall score falling by 2.4% from the previous year to 0.36. It placed 30th among 34 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting the depth of its institutional weaknesses relative to regional peers. The decline has persisted across multiple editions. Ethiopia ranked 129th out of 142 countries in 2023, with a score of 0.38, after placing 123rd out of 140 countries in 2022. In the 2024 edition, it ranked 130th out of 142 countries, recording a further 2.4% fall in its overall score. The successive declines point to a longer-term deterioration rather than a one-year fluctuation. They also come against a backdrop of armed conflicts, restrictions on civic freedoms and concerns over the independence and effectiveness of public institutions. Checks on government power, fundamental rights remain weak The 2025 index offers a detailed picture of the areas contributing to Ethiopia's poor performance. The country ranked 134th globally for constraints on government powers, 138th for fundamental rights, 135th for open government and 137th for regulatory enforcement. Its rankings were somewhat higher in civil justice, at 124th, and criminal justice, at 104th. It ranked 96th for absence of corruption. The figures suggest that the weakest areas extend beyond the operation of courts. They include the mechanisms through which government decisions are scrutinized, public institutions are held accountable and citizens exercise fundamental freedoms. The WJP's constraints-on-government-powers measure assesses whether those exercising public authority are bound by law and subject to institutional and non-governmental checks. These include legislative oversight, judicial limits on executive authority and the role of an independent press in holding government to account. Ethiopia's low ranking in this category is particularly significant given longstanding concerns about the relationship between political authority and independent institutions. The country's scores in open government and fundamental rights also point to persistent challenges involving access to information, civic participation and freedoms of expression, assembly and association. The index does not, by itself, establish the cause of every institutional weakness or determine responsibility for individual violations. It provides a comparative assessment based on surveys of households and legal practitioners and experts, capturing how the rule of law is experienced and perceived. Authoritarian practices have become entrenched In its 2026 global findings, the WJP identified the expansion of authoritarian practices, the narrowing of civic space and the weakening of checks and balances as the principal forces behind the continuing global decline. "Authoritarianism is no longer merely an emerging trend - it has become entrenched in many parts of the world," Alejandro Ponce, the WJP's executive director, said in the report's accompanying statement. The organization said more than 86% of countries and jurisdictions had experienced sustained five-year declines in at least one of three safeguards against authoritarian rule: constraints on government powers, open government or fundamental rights. The latest assessment also found that freedom of opinion and expression declined in 64% of countries, freedom of assembly and association in 67%, and civic participation in 65%. Judicial limits on government power deteriorated in 63% of countries, while civil justice weakened in 64% and criminal justice in 58%. The WJP said undue executive pressure and government interference were major drivers of institutional deterioration in both civil and criminal justice systems. Although these are global findings rather than Ethiopia-specific figures, they provide context for the challenges reflected in Ethiopia's repeated low rankings. The country's performance in constraints on government power, fundamental rights and open government places those concerns at the center of its rule-of-law record. Conflicts and restrictions on civic space form part of the wider context Ethiopia's ranking comes amid continuing insecurity and serious human rights concerns across several regions. Armed conflicts in Amhara, Oromia and parts of Tigray have contributed to a difficult environment for civilian protection, access to justice and the exercise of basic freedoms. Addis Standard has previously reported on extrajudicial killings, torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances, as well as restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly. A U.S. State Department assessment of Ethiopia's 2024 human rights record, reported by Addis Standard in August 2025, documented abuses attributed to state and non-state actors in the context of ongoing conflicts. The media environment has also remained under pressure. In March 2026, Addis Standard reported on an assessment by International Media Support documenting continued intimidation, detention and harassment of journalists in Ethiopia. The report recorded at least 44 journalists abducted or detained during 2025, compared with 43 in 2024. Such developments are relevant to the rule-of-law assessment because the index considers not only whether laws exist, but also how effectively institutions protect rights, enforce legal safeguards and constrain the exercise of public power. Rather, its indicators provide a broader framework for assessing institutional performance alongside other documented evidence. Regional position underscores Ethiopia's decline Ethiopia's 2025 position of 30th among 34 sub-Saharan African countries placed it near the bottom of the regional table. The WJP has reported broad deterioration across sub-Saharan Africa, although some countries have recorded improvements in particular years. Ethiopia's continued low placement nevertheless points to the difficulty of reversing the institutional weaknesses identified in successive editions. Globally, the 2026 index covers 143 countries and jurisdictions and draws on more than 215,000 household surveys and 3,400 surveys of legal practitioners and experts. It assesses eight dimensions: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice. Scores range from zero to one, with higher scores indicating stronger adherence to the rule of law. The annual index is designed to measure how people experience the rule of law in practice, rather than simply whether a country has laws, courts or formal constitutional protections with its findings offering a comparative view of the relationship between legal institutions, public accountability and everyday access to justice. Press Release October 21, 2026 Updated: October 21, 2026 Ethiopian Americans Urge African Union to Include Amhara People and All Major Stakeholders in Ethiopia’s Peace Process October 21, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Congress (SM/file) Washington Update By Mesfin Mekonen Washington, D.C. The Coalition of Ethiopian Americans Civic Organizations has called on the African Union (AU) to ensure that the Amhara people and other major stakeholders are meaningfully included in future peace negotiations aimed at resolving Ethiopia’s ongoing conflicts. In a formal appeal dated October 19, 2026, the coalition urged the AU to pursue a comprehensive, inclusive, and sustainable peace process that addresses the root causes of Ethiopia’s political instability, armed confrontations, and continuing humanitarian crisis. In a letter addressed to His Excellency Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the African Union Commission, the coalition emphasized that lasting peace in Ethiopia cannot be achieved without the meaningful participation of all major stakeholders affected by the country’s conflicts. The letter warned that excluding significant political, ethnic, and religious communities risks undermining the legitimacy and long-term success of peace initiatives. The coalition acknowledged the African Union’s leadership in facilitating the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement between the Ethiopian government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). The agreement was an important step toward ending the devastating war in northern Ethiopia. However, the coalition argued that the limited participation of other major stakeholders highlighted the need for a broader approach to peacebuilding across the country. Although the Pretoria Agreement addressed the conflict between its signatories, Ethiopia continues to face armed confrontations, displacement, insecurity, and serious human rights concerns in several regions. According to the coalition, a peace process that addresses only selected parties cannot resolve the wider political grievances, questions of representation, and security concerns affecting Ethiopia’s diverse population. Amhara Community’s Security and Human Rights Concerns The coalition expressed deep concern over reports of killings, forced displacement, attacks on civilians, and other serious human rights violations affecting the Amhara population. It noted that members of the community have raised longstanding concerns about their security, political representation, and treatment within Ethiopia. The letter also highlighted reports of attacks against Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church clergy, worshippers, and religious institutions. Such incidents, the coalition argued, threaten not only human life and property but also religious freedom, cultural heritage, and the social fabric of Ethiopian society. The coalition called for credible and impartial investigations into allegations of serious human rights violations, effective protection for civilians, and accountability for those responsible under applicable law. It also pointed to ongoing armed confrontations involving government forces and various armed groups, including Fano and factions associated with the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), as evidence of the complexity of Ethiopia’s security crisis. The coalition maintained that military action alone cannot resolve the political grievances and security concerns underlying these conflicts. Instead, it urged the African Union to support meaningful dialogue that addresses the root causes of violence and creates a foundation for peaceful coexistence. Seven Recommendations for Sustainable Peace In its appeal to the African Union Commission, the coalition outlined seven recommendations intended to strengthen the prospects for a comprehensive and lasting peace in Ethiopia. First, ensure the meaningful inclusion of the Amhara people. The coalition urged the AU to ensure that representatives capable of articulating the community’s political, security, and human rights concerns participate directly in peace negotiations. Such participation, it stressed, must be substantive rather than symbolic. Second, broaden participation to include all major stakeholders. The coalition called for an inclusive process involving affected communities, political parties, relevant armed actors, civil society organizations, religious institutions, women’s groups, and other stakeholders. It argued that a credible peace process must reflect Ethiopia’s diversity and recognize the legitimate concerns of communities throughout the country. Third, address the root causes of Ethiopia’s conflicts. The coalition urged negotiators to confront longstanding grievances concerning political representation, equality before the law, security, human rights, constitutional governance, and fundamental freedoms. Without addressing these underlying issues, the coalition warned, any agreement risks producing only a temporary cessation of hostilities rather than a durable settlement. Fourth, strengthen civilian protection and religious freedom. The letter called on all parties to protect civilians, prevent attacks on religious institutions, facilitate humanitarian assistance, and respect international human rights and humanitarian law. It also emphasized the need to protect communities facing violence, displacement, and threats to their religious freedom. Fifth, promote impartial investigations and accountability. The coalition called for credible and independent investigations into reported atrocities and serious human rights violations. It urged the African Union to encourage appropriate investigative mechanisms and accountability measures that apply fairly to all parties, regardless of political affiliation or identity. Sixth, support inclusive national dialogue and democratic reform. The coalition emphasized the need for a credible national dialogue that brings Ethiopia’s diverse communities together to address fundamental political disagreements peacefully. Such a process, it argued, should advance constitutional governance, the rule of law, democratic institutions, minority rights, and equal citizenship. Seventh, establish a comprehensive and sustainable peace framework. The coalition encouraged the African Union to work with the Ethiopian government, relevant political and community representatives, and international partners to develop a framework with clear commitments, mechanisms for monitoring implementation, and meaningful opportunities for affected communities to participate in decisions concerning their future. A Call for Stronger African Union Leadership The coalition stressed that Ethiopia’s continuing instability has consequences beyond its national borders, affecting regional security, humanitarian conditions, and stability throughout the Horn of Africa. As a founding member of the Organization of African Unity, the predecessor of the African Union, Ethiopia has historically played an important role in African diplomacy and continental affairs. The coalition argued that the AU has both a responsibility and an opportunity to help the country move away from armed conflict toward peaceful political coexistence. Achieving that objective, the letter emphasized, will require impartial mediation, broad stakeholder participation, respect for human rights, and a willingness to address the legitimate concerns of all affected communities. “There can be no lasting peace in Ethiopia without the meaningful inclusion of the Amhara population and other major stakeholders in the peace process,” the coalition emphasized in its appeal. The letter warned that excluding important communities risks perpetuating the grievances, political divisions, and security challenges that have contributed to Ethiopia’s recurring conflicts. The coalition therefore urged the African Union Commission to make inclusive participation a central principle of its engagement with Ethiopia and to encourage the establishment of a credible peace process that gives all affected communities a meaningful opportunity to shape their country’s future. International Engagement and Accountability In addition to addressing the African Union, the coalition’s letter was copied to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee. The outreach reflects the coalition’s effort to encourage African and international institutions to support a peace process that prioritizes civilian protection, accountability, national reconciliation, and democratic governance. The coalition stated its readiness to support constructive initiatives promoting peace, respect for human rights, and democratic institutions in Ethiopia. It also expressed hope that, under the leadership of the African Union Commission, a more inclusive and impartial process could help address the concerns of Ethiopia’s diverse communities and establish a foundation for lasting stability. Conclusion: Inclusion Is Essential to Lasting Peace Ethiopia’s path toward peace requires more than agreements between selected parties. It requires a process that recognizes the country’s diverse communities, addresses longstanding grievances, protects fundamental rights, and creates meaningful opportunities for political participation. The central message of the Coalition of Ethiopian Americans Civic Organizations is clear: a sustainable peace agreement must include the Amhara people and all other major stakeholders whose participation is necessary to resolve Ethiopia’s interconnected conflicts. For the African Union, the challenge is to help facilitate a peace process that goes beyond ending individual confrontations and addresses the broader political and security issues threatening the country’s future. An inclusive, impartial, and accountable approach would offer a stronger foundation for national reconciliation and peaceful coexistence. Exclusion, by contrast, risks leaving essential grievances unresolved and prolonging the cycle of conflict. As Ethiopia continues to confront serious challenges, the African Union’s leadership will be important in encouraging dialogue, protecting civilians, and supporting a credible political process. Lasting peace will depend on whether all affected communities have a meaningful voice in shaping Ethiopia’s future. The memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed Saturday in Mogadishu by Transport and Civil Aviation Minister Mohamed Farah Nuh, Somali Civil Aviation Authority Director General Ahmed Moallim Hassan and Kamil Alawadhi, IATA’s regional vice president for Africa and the Middle East. advertisements Under the agreement, the Somali Civil Aviation Authority will recognize the IATA Operational Safety Audit (IOSA) and the IATA Safety Audit for Ground Operations (ISAGO) as acceptable means of compliance with national regulations, complementing its own safety oversight functions. The programs will complement, rather than replace, the authority’s own regulatory and safety oversight functions. “Global safety standards are the cornerstone of efficient and safe operations. Through this MoU, we will work with the Somali CAA towards the continuous improvement of safety standards, promote the adoption of industry best practices, and foster a culture of safety across the aviation sector. This partnership reflects our mutual dedication to advancing aviation safety for the benefit of passengers, operators and the wider aviation industry in Somalia and Africa,” said Kamil Alawadhi, IATA’s Regional Vice President for Africa and Middle East. IOSA is an internationally recognized audit system designed to assess an airline’s operational management and control systems. More than 450 airlines are currently listed on the IOSA registry, and all IATA member airlines are required to maintain IOSA registration. ISAGO applies similar standardized oversight to companies providing ground-handling services at airports. IATA says the program is intended to reduce operational risks, improve consistency in ground handling and limit duplication between audits conducted by airlines, airports and regulators. The agreement forms part of IATA’s Focus Africa initiative, which includes efforts to improve aviation safety, infrastructure, connectivity and regulatory standards across the continent. The agreement signed in Mogadishu comes as authorities continue rebuilding a civil aviation system that was severely weakened after the collapse of the central government in 1991. The country has gradually reestablished national control over aviation functions, including management of Somali airspace and regulatory oversight of airlines and airports. Somali Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali met on Monday his Iraqi counterpart, Fuad Hussein, on the sidelines of the 52nd session of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad, according to Somalia’s Foreign Ministry. advertisements The two ministers discussed activating the Somalia-Iraq joint committee and broadening cooperation in key sectors, particularly agriculture, trade and other areas of economic exchange. Somalia also expressed interest in beginning exports of live animals to Iraq, a potentially significant market for a country where livestock remains one of the most important export industries. The Somali Foreign Ministry described the prospects for deeper economic cooperation between the two countries as promising and said both sides agreed on the need to accelerate the work of the joint committee. Ali also thanked Iraq for hosting the OIC meeting and reaffirmed Somalia’s commitment to strengthening relations with Baghdad. The talks were held as Iraq hosted foreign ministers and other delegates from OIC member states for the Oct. 17-18 meeting, which concluded with the adoption of the Baghdad Declaration and a series of resolutions on political, economic and humanitarian issues. Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein chaired the session as Baghdad assumed the presidency of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers for the coming period. Somalia relies heavily on livestock exports, particularly sheep, goats, cattle and camels, with Gulf and Middle Eastern markets serving as major destinations. Expanding access to Iraq would diversify those markets and could provide an additional outlet for Somali pastoralists and livestock traders. The meeting did not announce a date for the joint committee to convene or specify when livestock shipments to Iraq could begin. Uganda goalkeeper David Ssegirinya emerged as the decisive figure at Kigali Pele Stadium, making several important saves during the match before stopping three penalties in the shootout. advertisements Both teams had already secured qualification for the 2027 TotalEnergies CAF U-17 Africa Cup of Nations by reaching the regional final. Somalia created chances of its own during the match, with Abdullahi Hashi forcing a save from Ssegirinya from a free kick, while Asad Mohamed and Mohamud Osman missed opportunities late in the game. Uganda also threatened repeatedly, including a long-range effort from Sumaku Mutawakali that struck the crossbar. Neither side could score before the final whistle, sending the championship match directly to penalties. Ssegirinya then saved three Somali spot kicks as Uganda prevailed 6-5 to claim the regional title. He was later named goalkeeper of the tournament after conceding only once during the competition. “I am very happy with the players because we worked so hard, topped the group, beat Ethiopia in the semis and now lifted the trophy after winning on penalties,” Uganda coach Kingston Laryea said. Uganda captain Henry Muhoozi described the victory as a proud moment after leading his country to both the regional championship and qualification for next year’s continental tournament. “We are very proud of ourselves and thank everyone for the support,” Muhoozi said. Somalia coach Dadir Amin Ali praised his players for reaching the final and securing another appearance at the U-17 Africa Cup of Nations. “As a coach I am very proud of my boys because it has been real hard work,” Ali said. Somalia reached Monday’s final after eliminating host Rwanda 5-4 on penalties following a 1-1 semifinal draw. Mohamud Osman scored Somalia’s equalizer four minutes after Rwanda took the lead in the second half. Uganda qualified for the final with a 4-0 semifinal victory over Ethiopia. Rwanda secured the region’s third qualification place for the 2027 U-17 AFCON after beating Ethiopia 2-1 in the third-place playoff. somalia.content: Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 20, 2026 Nurto fled conflict in Baidoa and is struggling to support her seven children in Dadaab refugee camps/Ahmed Abdulahi/Ergo Families fleeing adversity in different parts of southern Somalia have been arriving in Kenya’s Dadaab refugee camps, where they find themselves with no means of making a living nor aid or support. They include families fleeing conflict in Baidoa, house demolitions by the Somali government in Mogadishu, and drought in their home areas. advertisements The new arrivals say they have received no reception support, shelter, or other forms of aid. Some are staying with relatives already struggling to make ends meet, while others have settled on their own on vacant land in Dadaab’s Ifo-2 camp. They lack food, housing, toilets and other basic services. Nurto Mohamed Ali, who arrived in Ifo-2 on 20 August, said her family had received no assistance and was struggling to meet basic needs. She is staying with relatives who arrived earlier. “Neighbours collect maize and cooking oil for us. That is how we are surviving now,” she said. “We have children who need food and bedding, but we have nothing to give them.” Nurto fled ongoing conflict in Baidoa between federal government forces and those loyal to the former South West State administration. She was a farmer raising her family on their two-hectare plot of land in Baidoa. Separated from her husband, she receives no support from him and is the sole income earner. In the refugee camp now, her seven children often go to bed hungry because she lacks food. They occupy a shelter made from plastic sheets, cloth and thorny branches in the yard of a relatives’ home – a household of 10. The days reach a scorching 37°C and the rainy season has begun. Nurto and her older children have to sleep outside without bedding while the youngest children cram themselves into the hut. Nurto said they had expected to receive assistance on arrival, including refugee registration cards, household items, and a house. She has received nothing. “We have no proper house, and even the people who arrived before us do not have one. The shelter situation is very difficult. We sleep on pieces of cloth and a small, broken mat,” she said. Other vulnerable new arrivals, including older people, people with disabilities, women and children, are finding no formal help in the camp, where some walk around daily asking more established residents for food. Hawo Mohamed Ali, her disabled husband, and their 10 children arrived in Ifo-2 on 1 August. They fled Mogadishu’s Hodan district after the government demolished their house, saying the land belonged to the state. They had lived in the house for 34 years without having formal land ownership documents. She said losing the home made it impossible for her family to remain in Mogadishu. “When we left and went outside, we found our land fenced off and surrounded by a wall,” she told Radio Ergo. “We were told the land would be measured and returned to us. Our houses were demolished using bulldozers, and we thought the land would be given back. Later, we were told it was government land and that we had to leave.” The demolition left Hawo’s family homeless and they decided their only option was to seek refuge in Dadaab. In Mogadishu, she earned a living selling meat and watermelon in local markets. In the refugee camp, however, they have not been registered and haven’t received aid cards or assistance. She looked for laundry work, but the jobs are irregular, so she has to ask others for help with food for her children. She lacks firewood and containers for collecting water. “The children’s father is disabled, and life is very difficult for us. My children are still young and have nothing here. We left our home and came to a place we do not know,” said Hawo, adding that the conditions in Dadaab were far worse than she had expected. The chairman of Hagardera camp, Khalif Dhubow Jelle, said the hardship facing new arrivals from Somalia had been brought to the attention of humanitarian agencies in the camps, but no effective response had followed. He recorded nearly 250 families having arrived from southern Somalia in the past three months. “Their living conditions are extremely poor. It is also the rainy season, yet these people have no shelter or place to stay. They are sitting in the open and have no food or water,” he said. The new arrivals are joining a refugee population already struggling with difficult living conditions because of reduced humanitarian aid and wider economic hardship across the camps. football.summary: الهلال السوداني حقق إنجازًا كبيرًا في مسيرته الكروية، حيث تمكن من الوصول إلى مراحل متقدمة في المنافسات القارية. اللاعب "غربال" كان له دور بارز في هذا النجاح، حيث أظهر مهاراته العالية وأداءه المتميز في المباريات. الجماهير تتطلع إلى المزيد من الإنجازات، مع آمال كبيرة في تحقيق الألقاب. الهلال يسعى لتعزيز مكانته في الساحة الرياضية، ويبدو أن الفريق في طريقه لتحقيق المجد الذي يطمح إليه.
